mcqNotes.13: Read Only Memory (ROM) is non-volatile permanent memory used to store essential startup firmware (such as the system BIOS/UEFI) that cannot be altered under normal operation.
mcqNotes.14: Cache memory is a small, ultra-fast static RAM buffer placed close to the processor to hold frequently accessed instructions and data, reducing memory latency.
mcqNotes.15: Dynamic RAM (DRAM) memory cells are fundamentally composed of a single transistor and a single storage capacitor, which requires periodic electrical refreshing to maintain its charge.
mcqNotes.16: Static RAM (SRAM) is built from multi-transistor flip-flop latches that do not require refreshing, providing the sub-nanosecond speeds necessary for CPU L1, L2, and L3 caches.
mcqNotes.17: In the multi-tier cache hierarchy, Level 3 (L3) cache is situated further from execution cores than L1 and L2, making it significantly larger in capacity but comparatively slower in access time.
mcqNotes.18: Compact Discs (CDs) utilize 780 nm infrared lasers, Digital Versatile Discs (DVDs) utilize 650 nm red lasers, and Blu-ray discs utilize 405 nm blue-violet lasers. The board key accepts option C (I and II).
mcqNotes.19: Solid-state flash storage (including SD cards and SSDs) traps electrons within floating-gate or charge-trap transistor memory cells to retain data without continuous power.
mcqNotes.20: CPU registers are high-speed, on-chip storage locations that temporarily hold immediate operands, memory addresses, and data words undergoing active execution by the ALU.
mcqNotes.21: The Accumulator (AC) is the primary general-purpose arithmetic register in a CPU designed to store intermediate calculation results and operand data.
mcqNotes.22: During the execute phase of the machine instruction cycle, the control unit and ALU interpret the decoded operation and carry out the required instruction tasks.
mcqNotes.23: The CPU contains the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), control unit (CU), registers, and internal buses; the system unit is the external chassis housing the motherboard and power supply.
mcqNotes.24: In standard x86 and accumulator architectures, the base register (BX) and counter register (CX) serve as versatile general-purpose data and indexing registers.
mcqNotes.25: Data transfer instructions (such as MOV, LOAD, and STORE) transfer byte or word values between CPU internal registers and system RAM.
mcqNotes.26: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) transmits uncompressed digital high-definition video and multi-channel audio over a single unified cable.
mcqNotes.27: A Gigabit Ethernet Network Interface Card (NIC) connects a computer via twisted-pair copper or fiber cabling to achieve wired local network throughput up to 1000 Mbps.
mcqNotes.28: SIMM modules feature a 32-bit data path, whereas modern DIMMs incorporate electrical contacts on both sides to provide an independent 64-bit wide data path.
mcqNotes.29: The physical system unit fundamentally comprises the protective enclosure (casing), power supply unit (PSU), and main circuit board (motherboard).
mcqNotes.30: The fundamental objective of computer networking is enabling seamless digital communication between nodes and facilitating shared access to hardware and data resources.
mcqNotes.31: A Body Area Network (BAN) interconnects low-power smart sensors and wearable medical or fitness devices within a range of centimeters to a few meters around the human body.
mcqNotes.32: The 4-layer TCP/IP protocol architecture combines the functions of the OSI Session, Presentation, and Application layers into a single comprehensive Application layer.
mcqNotes.33: A mesh network topology interconnects every node with multiple redundant point-to-point links, ensuring alternate transmission paths if any single link fails.
mcqNotes.34: In a ring topology, each device connects sequentially to exactly two neighboring nodes in a closed loop, circulating data packets in a unidirectional or bidirectional ring.
mcqNotes.35: Bluetooth is a short-wavelength UHF radio technology designed specifically for ad-hoc personal area network (PAN) device communication within approximately 10 meters.
mcqNotes.36: Infrared and wireless optical/RF networks allow mobile devices to join and communicate without altering or laying new physical copper or fiber cable connections.

mcqNotes.39: Global Positioning System (GPS) space-based trilateration enables receivers to pinpoint real-time geographic coordinates, altitude, and navigation headings anywhere on Earth.

**THREE Differences Between DRAM and SRAM (3 Marks):**

| S.No. | DRAM (Dynamic RAM) | SRAM (Static RAM) |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1** | **Internal Construction:** Constructed using a single transistor and a single storage capacitor per memory cell. | Constructed using multiple transistors (typically 4–6 flip-flop transistors) per memory cell without capacitors. |
| **2** | **Refreshing Requirement:** Requires continuous, periodic electrical refreshing because capacitors gradually leak charge. | Does not require electrical refreshing; data remains stable as long as power is maintained. |
| **3** | **Access Speed & Latency:** Slower access times (20–60 ns) with higher latency; used for primary system memory. | Much faster access times (1–10 ns) with ultra-low latency; used for CPU L1, L2, and L3 cache memory. |

*(Award 1 mark for each accurate, clearly contrasted point of difference up to 3 marks. Alternative: DRAM has higher packaging density and lower cost per bit; SRAM has lower density and higher cost per bit.)*

**Functions of Internal Buses (3 Marks):**
- **Data Bus:** A bidirectional pathway that carries actual data words, instruction opcodes, and operand values between the CPU, system memory (RAM), and peripheral I/O interfaces. Bus width (e.g. 32-bit or 64-bit) determines data throughput per clock cycle. *(1 Mark)*
- **Address Bus:** A unidirectional pathway driven by the CPU that carries the binary physical memory address or I/O port address specifying where data is to be retrieved from or stored to. Bus width ($2^n$) defines the maximum addressable memory space. *(1 Mark)*
- **Control Bus:** A set of signal lines that transmit timing and command control signals (e.g., Memory Read, Memory Write, I/O Read, I/O Write, Clock, and Interrupt Requests) from the CPU to synchronize bus operations across all connected modules. *(1 Mark)*

**Server Memory Upgrade (3 Marks):**
- **i. Memory Module Used:** **Dual Inline Memory Module (DIMM)** (specifically Registered / Buffered ECC DDR DIMMs for enterprise servers). *(1 Mark)*
- **ii. TWO Reasons in Support of DIMM (2 Marks):**
  1. **64-bit Independent Data Bus Path:** DIMMs feature independent electrical contacts on both sides of the module to provide a full 64-bit wide data bus (compared to older 32-bit SIMMs), doubling data transfer throughput per memory access. *(1 Mark)*
  2. **High Capacity, Multi-channel & ECC Support:** DIMMs accommodate significantly higher memory densities, support multi-channel interleaving, and feature Error-Correcting Code (ECC) architecture critical for detecting and correcting single-bit memory corruptions under demanding concurrent server workloads. *(1 Mark)*

**Wireless Communication Definitions (3 Marks):**
- **i. Radio signals:** Electromagnetic waves propagated through free space within the radio frequency spectrum ($3\text{ kHz}$ to $300\text{ GHz}$), modulated to transmit data, voice, or multimedia information without physical guided conductors. *(1 Mark)*
- **ii. Radio transceivers:** An integrated electronic hardware unit that combines both radio transmitter and radio receiver circuits, sharing a common housing and antenna to facilitate bidirectional wireless transmission. *(1 Mark)*
- **iii. Access point (WAP):** A dedicated networking device connected to a wired local area network (LAN) that transmits and receives radio frequency signals, enabling wireless-capable client devices (laptops, phones) to access network resources. *(1 Mark)*

**EITHER a. TCP/IP Protocol Architecture (7 Marks):**

**i. Functions of Each Layer (4 Marks):**
1. **Application Layer:** Provides direct network communication interfaces and protocol services to end-user software applications, handling high-level data formatting, encoding, and dialogue control (e.g., web, mail, file transfer). *(1 Mark)*
2. **Transport Layer:** Establishes reliable or datagram host-to-host end-to-end communication channels. It handles packet segmentation, reassembly, flow control, port-based multiplexing, and error recovery (via TCP or UDP). *(1 Mark)*
3. **Internet Layer:** Responsible for logical addressing (IP addresses) and routing packets across interconnected, heterogeneous networks, encapsulating transport segments into IP packets. *(1 Mark)*
4. **Network Access Layer:** Manages physical hardware addressing (MAC addresses), framing of IP packets into physical network frames, and transmitting raw bits as electrical, optical, or radio signals across the physical medium. *(1 Mark)*

**ii. Protocol Names for Any Three Layers (3 Marks):**
- **Application Layer:** HTTP / HTTPS / FTP / DNS / SMTP. *(1 Mark)*
- **Transport Layer:** TCP / UDP. *(1 Mark)*
- **Internet Layer:** IP (IPv4 / IPv6) / ICMP / ARP. *(1 Mark)*

7b.solution:
**OR b. Global Positioning System (GPS) (7 Marks):**

**i. Description of GPS (1 Mark):**
- A space-based satellite navigation system comprising a constellation of at least 24 orbiting satellites broadcasting synchronized radio signals, allowing terrestrial receivers to calculate their exact three-dimensional coordinates (latitude, longitude, altitude) and precise time through trilateration. *(1 Mark)*

**ii. THREE Points of Importance (3 Marks):**
1. **Accurate Turn-by-Turn Navigation:** Powers real-time vehicular, marine, and aviation navigation, optimizing routes and monitoring traffic. *(1 Mark)*
2. **Emergency Response and Tracking:** Enables first responders to locate 911 callers, track emergency vehicles, and direct search-and-rescue teams during natural disasters. *(1 Mark)*
3. **Precision Surveying and UTC Time Synchronization:** Supplies millimeter-precision geographic data for engineering construction and provides global atomic clock time synchronization essential for banking networks and electrical power grids. *(1 Mark)*

**iii. THREE Limitations of GPS (3 Marks):**
1. **Line-of-Sight Blockage:** Microwave signals cannot penetrate dense buildings, tunnels, underground structures, or deep underwater environments, and are degraded in urban canyons. *(1 Mark)*
2. **Susceptibility to Jamming and Spoofing:** Weak incoming satellite signals can be blocked by deliberate local radio interference (jamming) or falsified by malicious signal simulators (spoofing). *(1 Mark)*
3. **Atmospheric Delays and Power Demand:** Ionospheric and tropospheric variations introduce propagation delays that degrade accuracy, while continuous satellite tracking causes high battery consumption on mobile devices. *(1 Mark)*
